stories.title: Support ws:// transport for DHT-discovered relays
stories.description: Extend the relay WebSocket transport to accept ws:// (plaintext) connections for relay URLs obtained from DHT-resolved DID documents (§10.12.6). The SDK MUST reject ws:// relay URLs obtained from .well-known/scp or any non-DHT source. MLS provides the confidentiality boundary; TLS on a dumb pipe is defense-in-depth, not the security layer. This enables self-hosted relays behind NAT with no domain to be reachable without requiring TLS certificates.

stories.title: Implement did_routing_id derivation function
stories.description: Implement the did_routing_id derivation (§3.10.2): SHA-256("scp:did:" || did_string). This is a pure function with no dependencies — the building block for relay-based DID resolution.

stories.title: Implement DID document PUBLISH to SCP relays via RepublishManager
stories.description: Extend RepublishManager to publish DID documents to SCP relays using the existing PUBLISH operation (§3.10.5). DID documents are published as standard blobs with routing_id = did_routing_id(did_string) and blob_ttl = 604800 (7 days). Identity owners SHOULD publish to their own relays plus bootstrap relays. RepublishManager schedules relay republishing on a 6-day cycle (1-day margin before TTL expiry). Publishing to both SCP relays and Mainline DHT is a MUST per the anti-segmentation invariant (§3.10.6). Each layer receives its OWN encoding under its OWN signature and its OWN sequence number (§3.10.5, §18.2.2A): the relay layer receives the full document as RFC 8785 canonical JSON, and Mainline receives the DNS-encoded bootstrap core (§18.2.2C). This story previously assumed one encoding published to both layers; the two-encoding amendment removed that assumption from §3.10.5, which is why the status returned to pending. The Mainline encoder itself is a separate story; this story consumes it.

stories.title: Implement DID document QUERY from SCP relays
stories.description: Implement relay-based DID document resolution using the existing QUERY operation (§3.10.4). The resolver computes did_routing_id, queries known SCP relays (the identity's relays if known, else bootstrap relays), verifies the BEP44 signature against the public key encoded in the DID string, and checks seq against the last sequence number it observed ON THE RELAY LAYER for this DID (§3.10.4 step 4c). This is the relay layer of the dual-layer resolution protocol, and it carries the full DID document as canonical JSON (§18.2.2A). Cache results per §9.10.7 (24h active, 7d inactive), keyed per (DID, layer). This story previously keyed the sequence check and the cache by DID alone and sent limit = 1; §3.10.4 now keys both per layer and §3.10.2 specifies limit = N (N = 16), which is why the status returned to pending.

stories.title: Implement DidResolver trait with parallel dual-layer resolution
stories.description: Implement the DidResolver trait (§3.10.10) that composes relay QUERY with DhtClient::resolve() for parallel dual-layer resolution. Both layers are queried in parallel via tokio::join! with the per-layer 5-second timeout §3.10.4 states. Valid means the BEP44 signature verifies AND the sequence number is >= the last sequence number this resolver observed ON THE SAME LAYER (§3.10.4 step 4c). The two layers carry different encodings under different signatures (§18.2.2A), so selection is per layer and never across layers (§3.10.4 step 5, §3.10.7): the relay layer answers for the full document, Mainline answers for the bootstrap core (§18.2.2C), and a resolver MUST NOT compare one layer's sequence number against the other's. ResolutionSource tracks which layer served the result, and DocumentCompleteness tells the caller whether it holds the full document or the bootstrap core. This story previously specified cross-layer highest-sequence-wins; the amendment that removed that rule from §3.10.7 also removed it here, which is why the status returned to pending.
acceptanceCriteria: DidResolver trait defined with resolve(&self, did: &str) -> Result<Option<ResolvedDidDocument>>

ResolvedDidDocument is an ENUM with two variants carrying two different types (§3.10.10): Full { document: DidDocument, seq, source } and BootstrapCore { core: BootstrapCore, seq, source }. It is NOT a struct with a sibling completeness flag — that shape let a caller read a relay-layer field off a bootstrap-core result and receive an empty value, which is the mistake this type exists to prevent

BootstrapCore is a distinct struct carrying identity_key, active_key, pre_rotation_commitment and relays, and NO field for any relay-layer entry, so reading SCPCapabilities off a bootstrap-core resolution fails to compile; a Mainline resolution returns the BootstrapCore variant and a relay resolution returns Full
ResolutionSource enum has ScpRelay { relay_url: String }, MainlineDht, and Cache variants
Parallel query: both SCP relay and DHT resolution initiated concurrently via tokio::join!
The resolver keeps one last-known sequence number per (DID, layer) pair, and rejects a record whose seq is lower than the number observed on the layer that served it (§3.10.4 step 4c)
The resolver never compares a relay-layer sequence number against a Mainline sequence number, and never discards one layer's record because the other returned a higher number (§3.10.4 step 5c)
Within the relay layer, when more than one valid record is returned, the highest-seq valid record wins (§3.10.4 step 5a)

When both layers answer, the relay-layer record is the answer WHATEVER the caller asked for, including a caller needing only a bootstrap-core element such as #active (§3.10.4 step 5d, §3.10.1) — a fixed precedence, not a sequence comparison
DidMethod::resolve() continues to work for single-layer Mainline resolution and returns the BootstrapCore variant (no regression)
Unit test: relay responds with a valid full document, Mainline returns nothing — the relay result is used and is the Full variant
Unit test: Mainline responds, relay returns nothing — the Mainline result is used and is the BootstrapCore variant
Unit test: both layers respond with different sequence numbers — neither record is discarded, and the relay record answers a full-document request
Unit test: a relay record whose seq is below the cached RELAY seq is rejected, while a Mainline record at that same seq is accepted because its own layer's cached seq is lower
Unit test: one layer fails, the other layer's result is accepted in its own variant; and a test asserts a caller needing only #active still receives the relay record when both layers answered

stories.description: Symmetric NAT detection requires comparing external addresses from multiple STUN servers (§10.12.9 threat model). This story adds divergence detection: query at least 2 STUN servers, compare external addresses, and classify as symmetric if they diverge.

stories.title: Implement per-layer healing: re-publish a layer's own encoding back to that layer when it serves a stale record
stories.description: Per §3.10.7, healing is per layer and it is a MAY. When a layer returns a record whose sequence number is lower than the number the resolver already holds for THAT layer, the resolver MAY re-publish that layer's own current encoding back to that same layer. A resolver MUST NOT copy one layer's bytes to the other layer: the full JSON document exceeds Mainline's 1,000-byte cap and the DNS-encoded bootstrap core is not what the relay layer is authoritative for (§18.2.2A, §18.2.2D). This story previously specified cross-layer healing — republishing the fresher document to whichever layer returned the stale one — which the two-encoding amendment removed from §3.10.7 as unperformable, so this story's status returned to pending. No production code performs healing today: DualLayerResolver::new sets healing_publisher to None at every construction site, and with_healing is called only from the crate's own test module, so the capability is honestly absent rather than stubbed.
acceptanceCriteria: When a relay returns a relay-layer record whose seq is lower than the resolver's cached relay-layer seq, the resolver MAY re-publish its cached relay-layer encoding to that relay
When Mainline returns a record whose seq is lower than the resolver's cached Mainline seq, the resolver MAY re-publish its cached bootstrap-core encoding to Mainline
The resolver never publishes a relay-layer encoding to Mainline, and never publishes a bootstrap-core encoding to a relay — a test asserts each direction is refused
The resolver never triggers healing from a cross-layer sequence comparison, because §3.10.7 forbids that comparison
Healing is asynchronous (does not block the resolve call)
Healing is best-effort (failure is logged, not propagated)

A resolver that never heals is conformant, and a test covers the healing_publisher: None path returning results unchanged
actionItems: Add a per-layer healing trigger in DualLayerResolver keyed on that layer's own cached seq
Implement async republish of a layer's own encoding back to that layer
Wire RepublishManager or a dedicated healing publisher, and keep the no-healing path conformant
Add tests for both layers, plus tests asserting no cross-layer copy occurs
stories.result: The shipped implementation no longer satisfies this story, and the story still asks for the capability. The earlier work built cross-layer healing: DualLayerHealingPublisher + DualLayerResolver integration, republishing the fresher document to the stale layer on cross-layer seq divergence via tokio::spawn, with tests seq_divergence_triggers_healing and healing_failure_logged_not_propagated. §3.10.7 removed cross-layer healing as unperformable under two encodings and kept per-layer healing as a MAY, so this story was re-scoped rather than superseded: its acceptance criteria now describe per-layer healing, and five of the nine are unmet. Nothing built from it reaches production either way: DualLayerResolver::new sets healing_publisher to None at every construction site, and with_healing is called only from the crate's own test module.

stories.title: Implement BRIDGE_REGISTER authentication with routing ID ownership proof
stories.description: BRIDGE_REGISTER currently accepts any routing_id without authentication (§10.12.4). An attacker can register arbitrary routing IDs and intercept traffic meant for the legitimate self-hosted relay. This story adds signature-based authentication: the BRIDGE_REGISTER message must include an Ed25519 signature proving the sender owns the DID that maps to the claimed routing_id.
